item.research_question: To evaluate the feasibility of producing aluminium matrix composites reinforced with different volume fractions of AlCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy particulates using powder metallurgy, and to study the effect of particulate volume on microstructure, mechanical properties, wear response, and corrosion resistance.
item.material_system: Aluminium AA-1050 (99.5%) matrix reinforced with AlCrFeMnNi HEA particulates at 1 vol.%, 3 vol.%, and 5 vol.%
item.processing_route: Powder metallurgy route: HEA produced via vacuum arc melting (5 remeltings) and crushed by dry grinding in a planetary mill (10 min work/20 min pause, 4 cycles); powders mixed with methanol, pressed into 14 mm pellets, then sintered in a hot press furnace at 550 °C for 1 h under argon, followed by application of 6500 N load raised at 100 N/min and held for 30 min.
item.test_conditions: Nanoindentation at 1000 nm depth with loads up to 196.13 mN at speeds of 13.3240 mN/s and 2.2207 mN/s with 30 s hold; sliding wear at 10 m/s for 1000 m distance using 100Cr6 steel ball; corrosion testing in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at pH 7 with 10 mV/min scan rate.
key_findings: SEM analysis showed reinforcing particle area coverage of 2.04% for 1 vol.%, 4.31% for 3 vol.%, and 7.18% for 5 vol.% composites.
Hardness increased with reinforcement content; the matrix exhibited lower hardness values compared to the HEA particulates (around 57 HRC).
Creep depth of the matrix was considerably higher than the HEA phase, with stress exponent (n) values of 30–35 for the matrix and 58–86 for the HEA.
Wear rates were lowest for samples with increased reinforcement, while the 1% sample showed the highest mass loss in the initial 200 m.
Wear mechanisms included abrasive wear (grooves), oxidative wear (oxide layers), and delamination wear (flake-like debris).
Corrosion curves showed a sustained flat gradient and negative hysteresis loops, indicating susceptibility to localised corrosion controlled by the matrix.
No secondary intermetallic phases or voids were observed at the particle-matrix interface in the 5 vol.% composite.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the increased hardness and wear resistance to the presence of hard HEA particles restricting mass movement and acting as barriers to crack propagation. Creep behavior is explained by dislocation mobility and the complex multi-phase nature of the HEA, where multiple interfaces at lower loading speeds may block dislocations, increasing the required load. Corrosion is driven by galvanic coupling where noble elements (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mn) in the HEA particles cause selective dissolution of the Al matrix at the interface.
item.limitations: The text states that 'further investigation is required to ascertain' the reversed loading behavior of the HEA reinforcement at lower speeds compared to previous work. Additionally, the corrosion performance was found to be 'not affected by the increasing volume of the reinforcement,' limiting the ability to tune corrosion resistance via volume fraction in this specific system.
item.future_work: The authors state that 'further investigation is required to ascertain' the reasons behind the reversed loading behavior of the HEA reinforcement at lower speeds, specifically regarding the role of multiple phases and interfacial boundaries.
quotes: The sintering stage was carried out in the following steps: First, the temperature was raised to 550 °C with a step of 50 °C/min with inert atmosphere using argon gas.
The n exponent is directly related to the creep behaviour: the higher its value, the more difficult for the creep phenomena to take place.
The corrosion behaviour was mainly controlled by the corrosion of the Al matrix.
